stories.headline: Why Man United are so bad at hiring managers post-Ferguson
stories.summary: This week marks 40 years since Manchester United hired Sir Alex Ferguson as their manager. It was the last time the club made the right appointment.
stories.body:
Manchester United mark a big anniversary later this week: it's 40 years since they last made the right decision on a managerial appointment.

They have become the club that always gets it wrong. Jürgen Klopp, Mauricio Pochettino and Thomas Tuchel have all spoken to the United hierarchy in recent years. But for one reason or another, they have all taken their coaching talents elsewhere.

As current boss Michael Carrick lurches from one bad result to another and with United hovering one place above the Premier League relegation zone having won just once in the league all season, Friday's anniversary of Alex Ferguson's arrival at Old Trafford in November 1986 might just coincide with the club's latest roll of the managerial dice.

- Make no mistake: Man United are in a relegation battle

- Transfer rumors, news: Man United meltdown edition. USMNT's Balogun linked

- Are Man City fans right? Is Premier League 'Red Cartel' out to get them?

Sources have told ESPN that Carrick, who signed a two-year contract in May after guiding United to UEFA Champions League qualification as interim manager last season, is likely to remain in charge for Tuesday's European game against AS Roma and Sunday's Premier League meeting with Aston Villa. But there are no guarantees after a nine-game winless run. The 45-year-old's job is hanging by a thread and with an international break looming beyond the Villa game, it is difficult to see the former Middlesbrough manager still being in charge for the trip to Liverpool on Nov. 22.

But can United be trusted to fire Carrick and replace him with a manager capable of bringing order, stability and most importantly, results, to soccer's most chaotic super-club?

Since Ferguson retired in 2013 after winning 28 major trophies in 27-and-a-half years at United, the club has hired seven permanent managers and none has come close to winning a Premier League or Champions League title.

ESPN has spoken to several people who have worked at United during the post-Ferguson years and been involved in managerial appointments. Each of the seven hires have been, in varying ways, flawed by the decision-making process at Old Trafford.

When United hired David Moyes to succeed Ferguson, it was claimed that he was hand-picked by the man he was replacing. The reality is that the Everton manager was the seventh choice, and Ferguson's intervention was simply a desperate move to find somebody with Premier League experience who could take over.

Sources have told ESPN that United approached Klopp, José Mourinho, Carlo Ancelotti, Pep Guardiola, Diego Simeone and Laurent Blanc before turning to Moyes. Mourinho, Ancelotti, Guardiola and Blanc had already agreed to take other jobs, while Klopp and Simeone were not interested.

When Moyes was fired 10 months into a six-year contract, United hired Netherlands coach Louis van Gaal, despite the former Ajax and Barcelona coach having been out of club management for three years. Prior to appointing Van Gaal, United executive vice-chairman Ed Woodward was rebuffed by Atlético Madrid coach Simeone again and famously failed to hire Klopp after the future Liverpool manager was unimpressed by his sales pitch of United being "an adult version of Disneyland."

When Van Gaal was sacked in May 2016, United hired Mourinho, who ultimately delivered two major trophies, a Premier League runners-up finish and a 58% win rate. But sources have said that Mourinho was hired despite co-chairmen Joel and Avram Glazer being urged by senior figures to appoint Pochettino. The future United States coach, then building a Tottenham Hotspur team that would challenge for Premier League title and reach the Champions League final, would miss out on the United job on two further occasions.

Sources have told ESPN the Mourinho hire was driven by the Glazers' determination to match Manchester City's move for Guardiola the same summer, but when Pochettino was the No. 1 choice to replace Mourinho two years later, a reluctance to engage in an expensive compensation battle with Spurs -- combined with Ole Gunnar Solskjær's remarkable results as interim manager -- prompted United to take the easy option and hand the job to their former player on a permanent basis.

If you are a spotting a theme with United's recruitment process, yes, it's that simple: draw up a list, miss out on the favoured candidates and hire somebody else.

Things changed slightly when Erik ten Hag was hired in the summer of 2022 after Woodward left and was replaced by CEO Richard Arnold. United installed Ralf Rangnick as interim coach while they underwent a "thorough recruitment process" to find the new permanent manager. Luis Enrique, then in charge of the Spain national team, was high on United's list, but would be ruled out due to his reluctance to leave the Spain job until after the 2022 FIFA World Cup.

Ten Hag and Pochettino became the final two candidates. Sources have told ESPN it was a close call, with Ajax coach Ten Hag regarded as a rising star and Pochettino, under contract at Paris Saint-Germain but facing a summer exit, likely to cost an eight-figure compensation package. Pochettino had his supporters within the United hierarchy, but the compensation figure tipped the process in favour of Ten Hag. History now shows the Dutchman to be another failed hire despite winning two major trophies before being fired in October 2024, four months after being handed a two-year contract by the new sporting hierarchy led by minority investor Sir Jim Ratcliffe.

Rewind to the end of the 2023-24 season, when Ten Hag only survived due to the supporters publicly backing him at Wembley after the FA Cup final win against Man City. At the time, United were openly speaking to candidates to replace him including Thomas Tuchel, Kieran McKenna and Roberto De Zerbi. Tuchel, who would become England manager in October 2024, spoke to United's senior figures more than once at that stage, and sources have said he was close to being offered the job before a decision was made to retain Ten Hag.

When Ten Hag was fired in October, he was replaced by Sporting CP coach Ruben Amorim, another rising star with no Premier League experience. Dan Ashworth, then sporting director, was dismissed during the process having earlier suggested Newcastle United's Eddie Howe for the job.

Amorim oversaw United's worst-ever Premier League season and had a win rate of just 38% when he was fired in January and replaced by Carrick. The former United midfielder was rewarded with a permanent contract this summer following his success in securing a third-place finish.

But Carrick was the latest inexperienced and inexpensive hire. Since Mourinho, United have not hired a manager with a proven Premier League track record -- Solskjær had six months at Cardiff City and was relegated -- and they have also ignored the clear trends that rival clubs have tapped into.

Spanish and German coaches have dominated the Premier League and Champions League over the past decade -- Guardiola (City) and Klopp (Liverpool) have won both, Luis Enrique (Paris Saint-Germain) has won back-to-back European crowns, Tuchel (Chelsea) and Hansi Flick (Bayern Munich) also won the Champions League and Mikel Arteta (Arsenal) won the Premier League.

United have never hired a German or a Spaniard as permanent manager and their last four appointments have been Premier League novices. Their hiring blueprint is deeply flawed.

So if Carrick goes, will United finally learn their lessons or make another mistake? The answer to that will make or break the club's future.

stories.headline: Aston Villa's Pau Torres relishing chance to face Lamine Yamal
stories.summary: Aston Villa's Pau Torres is relishing the prospect of going up against Barcelona star Lamine Yamal in Tuesday's Champions League showdown.
stories.body:
Aston Villa's Pau Torres is relishing the prospect of going up against Barcelona star Lamine Yamal in Tuesday's Champions League showdown.

Villa have won all three of their games in the competition this season heading into the encounter at the Camp Nou.

"When you play these matches, you always want to take on the best to see where you stand," the Spanish defender told Diario Sport.

"It'll be a pleasure to play against him [Yamal] and have to defend against him on a few occasions. He always catches you out; he's unpredictable, and often one player isn't enough to mark him. We'll have to be very alert when it comes to providing cover."

Yamal, 19, finished behind Real Madrid's Kylian Mbappé and winner Harry Kane of Bayern Munich in the Ballon d'Or race.

"[Ballon d'Or recipient] Harry Kane's stats have been excellent, but I wanted a Spaniard to win it and I think he [Yamal] deserved it," Torres said. "But if it wasn't to be this year, it will be very soon because Lamine is very close. I'm sure he'll maintain his form or improve on it."

Torres, however, would choose his former Villarreal teammate Rodri as the one player he would pick if his club could take one player from Barcelona.

Rodri, the 2024 Ballon d'Or winner, joined Barça in the summer from Manchester City after helping Spain lift the World Cup. "I'd take Rodri, because he completely dominates the midfield," Torres said. "He brings so much to the team both defensively and offensively, and in his position he's the best in the world."

- Barcelona boss Hansi Flick on Lamine Yamal: 'Easier' to substitute when he scores

- Jamie Carragher apologises for 'clumsy' Aston Villa comments after club threaten legal action

- Zion Suzuki fumble costs Aston Villa three points against resilient Fulham

Torres, in his fourth season at Villa, is dreaming big. A two-time Europa League under coach Unai Emery at Villarreal and Villa, Torres said: "I sometimes tell Unai that we've already won two Europa Leagues and that we have to try and go for the big one -- the Champions League."

"It's a very difficult task and we know we're by no means favourites or contenders for the title. But we know we can compete with anyone if we're at our very best."

stories.headline: How NBA title, MVP race has become wide open in two weeks
stories.summary: The NBA season is still young, but injuries and surprising developments have already changed narratives.
stories.body:
The 2026-27 NBA season was projected to be abnormally competitive, as previously rebuilding teams turned the corner and new draft lottery rules gave all 30 franchises an incentive to win.

At the top of the standings, though, three juggernaut rosters towered above the rest: the Oklahoma City Thunder and San Antonio Spurs, who both won more than 60 games before clashing in a seven-game conference finals last season, and the defending champion New York Knicks, who reeled off arguably the most dominant stretch in NBA history en route to the title.

Those three teams were excellent last season, and they returned 14 of their combined 15 starters this fall. So even as the rest of the league's floor rose, the highest ceilings still appeared to reside in New York City and the Southwest.

But surprising developments have changed that narrative less than two weeks into the new season and challenged the triumvirate's hegemony atop the league. Most importantly, a wave of injuries to star players already has altered the league's most important races.

Jump to a section:

How title odds have shifted

The injured stars so far

Is the MVP race wide open?

Scuffling preseason favorites
Oklahoma City opened its season with a firm statement of intent, with 12-point wins over the Spurs and Nuggets -- possibly the Thunder's closest competition in the West.

Then disaster struck. Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace both suffered potentially season-ending injuries in the same game, and Alex Caruso sprained his right ankle the following night. At the same time, Chet Holmgren suffered a patellar tendon tear in his right knee, which will sideline him for at least two months

So Oklahoma City has played its past couple games without four of its top six players, to predictable results: a 24-point loss in Dallas followed by a 21-point loss in Houston. The Thunder were outscored in all eight quarters across those two defeats.

The team will theoretically improve from their current doldrums once Caruso and Holmgren return, but the Thunder are in deep trouble on the perimeter without Williams and Wallace. They look far away from meaningful contention given their horrid spate of injuries.

But Oklahoma City isn't the only preseason favorite with more concerns now than two weeks ago. The Knicks are 2-4 and needed two big comebacks against Detroit and Chicago just to pick up their two wins. And the Spurs started a comparatively better 4-2, but they've looked out of sorts against the toughest competition they've faced and needed overtime to beat the injury-wracked Jazz.

It's very early, and those teams still have plenty of time to round into their best shape. But the title race already looks more open.

According to preseason projections by ESPN's Basketball Power Index (BPI), the Thunder and Spurs combined for a 50% championship probability. Add in the Knicks at 8%, and BPI gave those three favorites a roughly three-fifths chance to win the title. Yet their combined odds have since fallen to just 38%, and that's with the assumption that Wallace and Holmgren return before the playoffs.

Meanwhile, a series of second-tier contenders have started strong, which should increase their confidence that they can close the gap to the Thunder, Spurs and Knicks. The Rockets lead the way with a 5-1 record including wins over Oklahoma City and San Antonio. And in the Eastern Conference, the 76ers, Pistons and Celtics started a combined 16-3 -- meaning those three teams have fewer combined losses than the Knicks have by themselves.

That trend also serves as an argument for teams with strong rosters and ample draft assets, such as Houston and Detroit, to seriously consider making in-season trades with an eye on the Finals.

If the Thunder, Spurs and Knicks were all fully healthy and running roughshod over everyone in their paths, there might be some merit to the idea of keeping one's powder dry rather than making futile trades to try to catch the leading contenders. But if those teams still look more vulnerable than expected in a few months, the deadline could pack a more potent punch.

Even more injuries
Other prospective contenders have also borne the brunt of early-season injuries -- though none to the extent of Oklahoma City's nightmare.

Players who have already missed multiple games this season include Williams, Wallace, Caruso, Holmgren, Coby White, Kon Knueppel, Cameron Johnson, Jalen Duren, Alperen Sengun, Tyrese Haliburton, Ivica Zubac, Anthony Edwards, Paolo Banchero, Jalen Suggs, Kawhi Leonard and Jaren Jackson Jr.

That's more than a full roster's worth of stars (or star role players) who have suffered injuries within the first two weeks of the new season.

Discussion around the league generally points to increased pace and stress on the body as a reason for these injuries, while understanding that they're a mix of soft tissue problems and flukes -- like the collisions that sidelined Williams and Wallace.

It's also clear that there are no quick fixes. The NBA isn't slowing down, and more radical proposals that would change the sport to reduce wear and tear -- from a shorter schedule to 40-minute games -- are equally unlikely to happen any time soon. The injury issue is a figurative pain point for the league and a literal pain point for the players who keep getting hurt.

A (potentially) wide-open MVP race
Looking ahead to the remaining five months of the regular season, it's not just the title race that has opened to new challengers. The MVP race could also devolve into a free-for-all with one more injury.

The two most recent MVPs, who have finished first and second in the voting in some order three years running, have scuffled to start this season, with numbers well below their recent norms. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and Nikola Jokic perennially rank among the most productive, efficient stars in the league, but both have looked surprisingly mortal in the early going.

Put another way, Jokic and Gilgeous-Alexander finished first and second in player efficiency rating in each of the past two seasons, and they ranked first and third in 2023-24. Jokic has led the league in PER six years in a row.

Now, Jokic ranks 24th and Gilgeous-Alexander is 16th among qualified players in PER two weeks into this season.

Of course, these comparisons come after a very small sample of play -- but even then, the stars' relative struggles are unusual. Jokic, for instance, just completed his worst five-game stretch (as measured by box plus-minus) at any point in the season since 2020, before he won his first MVP.

For Gilgeous-Alexander, the Thunder's injury issues could counterintuitively give him a better chance to win his third straight MVP. Two-time winners are typically penalized -- if only unconsciously -- by voter fatigue, as no player has won three in a row since Larry Bird in the mid-'80s. However, if Gilgeous-Alexander can keep the Thunder near the top of the Western Conference standings and post his typically exemplary statistics without as much help from teammates, then he'd have a narrative boost to overcome that bias.

Yet if he and Jokic don't live up to the incredibly high standards they set while winning multiple MVPs apiece, then it seems far-fetched to think that either could claim another trophy this season.

That leaves Victor Wembanyama as the clear favorite, and betting odds reflect that status. He's responded by playing at an MVP level so far.

But remember, Wembanyama reached only the bare minimum number of games to qualify for awards last season, and he missed out in 2024-25. If he falls short of 65 games again, he could leave behind a truly wide-open race, with a whole host of viable second-tier candidates suddenly receiving real MVP consideration.

Could Luka Doncic finally receive his long-awaited MVP moment? Could Cade Cunningham, Jayson Tatum or Jalen Brunson become the first Eastern Conference perimeter players to win MVP since LeBron James in Miami? Could 19-year-old Cooper Flagg make a play at an historic award? (The answer is yes if he keeps dominating like he did in his first five games.)

The result is a season that brims with tremendous possibility -- even more than already seemed to be the case when the new year tipped off in October.

stories.headline: A child playcaller? The Bears' Ben Johnson was born for this
stories.summary: Johnson was in middle school when he first started diagramming plays, and we have one of the originals.
stories.body:
During the quarterback meeting the night before the Chicago Bears hosted the Philadelphia Eagles on Sept. 29, backup QB Case Keenum probed coach Ben Johnson over a play he wasn't certain would work.

Keenum, the 38-year-old journeyman who was starting in place of the injured Caleb Williams, was keen on everything about the play from the route to the protection, and particularly how it was designed, but he had reservations.

"It was a play Ben was very high on, and I loved it too, but I had some questions about it," Keenum said. "I don't want to say he talked me into it [that] night, but he assured me that it would be a good play. And, golly, he called it at the perfect time."

With a fresh set of downs at Philadelphia's 41-yard line and 5:55 on the clock in the third quarter, the Bears got a different look after the ball was snapped than what they had anticipated.

That's when Johnson's virtuosity as a play designer appeared.

The play was designed to allow the primary receiver to change in a matter of seconds based on the coverage. As he took off from the slot, Kalif Raymond realized quickly that he had become the primary, and the ball was coming his way.

As Eagles defenders vacated the middle of the field to cover three intermediate routes, Keenum fired a pass into an opening over the middle, where he found Raymond wide-open. The catch-and-run opportunity ended with a 41-yard touchdown as the Bears went on to record a 27-7 rout.

Those real-time adjustments that Johnson builds into his play designs are something players have come to appreciate. It's what separates him as a playcaller. It's what makes this Bears offense so dangerous.

"The cool part about Ben is he doesn't design plays within the box," Raymond said. "He'll design it based off the voids. Because he's not putting that conceptualized box that everybody pulls from on film, he starts creating his own play within the defensive scheme that you're about to go against.

"So now he's picking at your voids and [the defense has] to adjust in game."

The way Johnson designs plays for his offense has built the Bears into one of the NFL's most explosive units as Chicago is off to a 5-2 start. It's a reputation he earned around the league with a scheme rooted in unorthodox designs, trick plays and options, which allows everyone -- yes, everyone -- on offense to get involved.

"One of the coolest things about Ben is that when he installs a play, like, every play is going to work, every play is going to be an explosive, it doesn't matter if it's a short-yardage run, it doesn't matter if it's a 50-yard bomb," Williams said. "When we get out there, we have full faith in each other as a team, from coaches to players. When you have that, when you have a head ball coach like that, it goes a long way throughout the building."

Johnson's expertise as a play designer didn't begin when he started calling offenses of his own. His journey can be traced back to his very beginnings in football in Asheville, North Carolina, where he honed his ingenuity as a preteen who designed his own plays while still learning the game. From those roots to the biggest stage in the sport, Johnson has kept tinkering like a mad scientist in a lab, aiming to push the limits of his players and his scheme's capabilities.

"I can't say the words we use in the offensive meeting room because I'll go viral," Raymond said with a laugh. "It's a borderline between he's got a little bit of genius, a little bit of crazy, a little bit of aggressiveness."

Ben Johnson, the preteen play designer

Gail Johnson, a teacher and busy mom of three, found herself inquisitively staring at the scraps of paper scattered across the floor of her sons' bedroom.

The tiny scribbles etched in pencil were a part of some code Gail had regularly come across as she tidied up around the bunk beds shared by her young sons Ben and Kyle. Letters "E, T" in succession with a row of circles beneath them, each one containing a number. "QB" was labeled "1," "FB" was "2" and "TB" was "3." There was a long arrow pointing from the circle situated furthest to the left that traced upward before it veered slightly to its right.

Gail encountered these diagrams so often that she didn't think twice about throwing them away as she made beds and tossed clothes in the hamper. Until one day when Ben, a fifth-grader, inquired about their whereabouts.

From that point, Gail started saving these drawings and asked her son to explain what they meant. These were football plays, Ben told his mother, who would respond by asking what a specific play was designed to do. As Ben detailed the intent behind the collection of numbers, letters, shapes and lines, Gail transcribed.

Twins Right Rip 138 backside skinny post

Gail smiled as she recognized her handwriting that deciphered the code on one particular drawing, many of which are still housed inside a green folder labeled "keep 'ems" in the family's ranch-style home in Asheville.

"I knew then that his mind was working in that direction, that he was trying to be more creative with the plays that he was probably seeing himself run with his friends," Gail said. "He thought there's more out there, and [he] was going to start fiddling around with it."

In those days, Sundays were spent gathered around the television watching the San Francisco 49ers dominate the 1990s. The Niners were Don Johnson's favorite team. As a former college offensive coordinator and later a high school football coach, he appreciated San Francisco's West Coast offense and thought quarterback Joe Montana was "exceptional" for the way he operated within the scheme.

So did Ben, who would jump around the living room and try to throw a spiral with a football that barely fit in his hands while emulating his favorite quarterback.

On game days, Ben would sit next to his father and ask questions about what he saw unfolding on the screen. He wanted to know why a penalty was called and the reason why certain plays worked and others failed. There was a depth to the questions Ben asked at 10 and 11 years old that Don hadn't heard from the high school players he coached.

Ben's thirst for an understanding of the game he played from his youth through a walk-on career at the University of North Carolina grew as he began to sketch plays of his own. The lefty expanded his scribbles from scraps in pencil to colorful drawings in marker where the details jumped out immediately to his father. A misdirection play. An angled route where the quarterback throws to the split end, resulting in a touchdown. A play being blocked up by seven players -- "which is unusual," Don notes -- as a pass was thrown away from the play-action and resulted in a receiver being wide-open for a 60-yard touchdown.

"He wanted to impress his dad, I believe, and he did that with some of the things he [drew]," Don Johnson said.

Ben sought feedback from his father on the plays he designed. He not only wanted to know if they were legal within the rules of the game, but more importantly, whether Don thought they'd work.

"I tried to tell him I thought he did a pretty good job, but it confused me to see some of the things that he wrote down there," Don said. "So I had to talk with him a little bit more about, here's what actually you could probably do, and he listened very closely. He wanted to do the right thing."

It was like doing homework for Ben, who would sit at the oval wooden table adjacent to the kitchen and let his mind go to work. He took his affinity for designing plays and furthering his knowledge of offensive football as seriously as he did his academics. By the time he finished high school, he had quarterbacked A.C. Reynolds to a state championship and ranked top-five in his class academically.

His out-of-the-box thinking and progressive view for pushing the limits on offense were honed after he graduated from UNC and rose from a graduate assistant at Boston College to a position coach in Miami to getting to call his own scheme for the Detroit Lions. His path as a play designer and caller can be traced back to these vintage mementos that spark the now head coach of the Bears to ask a question out loud as he reunites with the drawings he once slaved over some 30 years ago

"I hope there's 11 on the field on both teams," Ben said with a smile.

Johnson's ingenuity in action

The play known as "Stumblebum" was masterminded by Johnson in his final season as Detroit's OC. It featured quarterback Jared Goff faking a stumble as he dropped back while running back Jahmyr Gibbs dove to the turf. Meanwhile, everyone up front yelled "fumble."

It was one the Lions repped for weeks in practice before they traveled to Soldier Field for a late December 2024 meeting with the Bears. If executed properly, then-Lions wide receivers coach Antwaan Randle El knew this unconventional play could break a game open.

"You can't put anything past us in terms of what we put in," said Randle El, who is now Johnson's right-hand man as the receivers coach and assistant head coach for the Bears. "If it looks like it is a possibility to try and do it, we're going to try and do it."

The design of the ruse worked as it grabbed the eyes and attention of Chicago defenders and allowed tight end Sam LaPorta to slip wide-open downfield for a 21-yard touchdown reception. The celebration was so raucous on the Lions' sideline that Randle El couldn't hear whether Johnson had sent out the kicking unit or whether Detroit was going to cap off the touchdown with a 2-point conversion. (They went for the extra point.)

The celebration was what caught the eye of Bears general manager Ryan Poles, whose team now trailed by 20 points early in the third quarter. Weeks ahead of when he would lead Chicago's head coaching search after the Bears fired Matt Eberflus in Nov. 2024, Poles saw Johnson making the type of statement that catapulted him to the top of Poles' list, which included 16 other candidates who interviewed for the job.

"There's a couple playcallers in the league during my time doing this that going against them, I felt helpless," Poles said. "And it's like, why is everybody open? How do we stop this? It's Ben and it's Kyle Shanahan. Those are the two guys that I've watched that just puts you in a really bad mood watching the game and going against them."

Poles felt vexed by what he witnessed Johnson's offense do to the Bears. At the same time, he had "a little grin" on his face seeing the genius of Johnson's play design in action, knowing what it could do for his team.

"If he's got you on the ropes, he wants to put your lights out," Poles said. "You could feel that mentality come out in his playcalling."

His creativity shines in moments when Johnson leans on the unexpected to catch his opponent off guard.

During Chicago's win over the Green Bay Packers in the playoffs, Johnson sent offensive lineman Theo Benedet on a post route as the Bears began their second-half comeback. The 6-foot-7, 304-pound tackle clocked over 16 miles per hour as he ran downfield, which forced the Packers to account for something they weren't expecting.

"The thing with him is he installs [plays] completely earnestly as if it's just a regular outside zone play," Benedet said. "So you're almost sitting there trying not to laugh and take it serious because you know it is to him."

Johnson's play designs that translate into playcalls don't have a 100% hit rate. Sometimes it's the ones that don't work that hold a lasting impact. In the Bears' 30-24 win over the Patriots in Week 7, the offense was flagged for an illegal handoff when Caleb Williams took a snap and handed the ball forward to left guard Joe Thuney, whose 4-yard run deep in New England's red zone was negated.

The ball needed to be handed backward for the play to be legal, and the way the Bears had run it in practice led to touchdowns. Still, Johnson was anything but discouraged as he went back to the drawing board, readying himself for the next opportunity to put his creativity to the test.

"It's one of those things, shooters shoot," Johnson said. "We shot, we missed. So, keep it moving."

stories.headline: MLB offseason buzz: Intel on Skubal, free agency, trade rumors
stories.summary: Who could land Tarik Skubal? Which ace could be traded? Here's the latest as the hot stove ignites.
stories.body:
The MLB hot stove season has arrived!

With players becoming free to sign with any team they choose today (free agency officially begins Monday at 5 p.m. ET), we asked our MLB reporters to open their notebooks with all of the intel they collected from execs, agents and other baseball insiders during the 2026 MLB postseason.

What is the early word on top free agent Tarik Skubal? Would the Tampa Bay Rays trade ace Drew Rasmussen on the heels of their World Series run? What will the New York Yankees, Los Angeles Dodgers and Chicago Cubs do after their playoff exits? And which other teams are generating the most buzz across the industry?

Here is what we're hearing as the hot stove ignites.

What are you hearing about Tarik Skubal as his free agency begins?

Jeff Passan: Skubal is far and away the best player in this class, and the expectation is he will sign before the Dec. 1 lockout. The two most obvious suitors are the two teams with the highest payrolls in baseball: The Los Angeles Dodgers and New York Mets. There are bound to be others. The Chicago Cubs badly want Skubal. They also are skeptical that they will be willing to compete at the sort of dollars Skubal is expected to get -- well in excess of $300 million, potentially in the $400 million-plus range. With Michael King and Nick Pivetta being free agents, the San Diego Padres need a rotation anchor, and arguably the best pitcher in baseball would more than suffice.

Others will join the foray, at the very least showing interest and perhaps joining the bidding. Either way, coming off another excellent season, Skubal will set a new record for a starting pitcher contract. The only question is how big it will be.

Alden Gonzalez: All things being equal -- and by "all things" I, of course, mean "money" -- my sense is Skubal would love to return to the Dodgers. He truly seemed to relish his 2½ months in Los Angeles. He loved the culture, particularly being among so many established, veteran players who were singularly focused on winning. He became besties with Blake Snell, was awed by the organization's resources and, overall, seemed to fit in seamlessly. But it's going to come down to price. And whether the Dodgers would be willing to match Steve Cohen's Mets or any other suitors that materialize given the threat of a salary cap remains to be seen.

Which other free agents are generating the most early buzz?

Buster Olney: Skubal is a market of one -- I've had a couple of folks estimate he'll get something north of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, in a six- or seven-year deal, with the usual suspects bidding against each other -- but behind him is a range of good veteran starting pitchers who will come off the board before the lockout.

Michael King, Clay Holmes, Nick Martinez and Tyler Mahle are among the starters who probably will have offers to accept, if they choose to wrap up their negotiations in November, because they're all in line to have good short-term compensation that teams can absorb no matter what financial system is in place next year. The playoffs and World Series served as a one month-long advertisement for Martinez, because not only did he pitch well and take the ball on short rest, but so much was said about how his clubhouse presence was difference-making for the Rays.

Seiya Suzuki might have the most leverage of the position players to sign, given that he's a right-handed power bat in a market starved for players like him.

Jesse Rogers: There were a slew of starters who were moved at the deadline in need of new homes now that they're free agents. Rays star Freddy Peralta likely improved his position in the market more than anyone considering his performance in Tampa. The same could be said of Padres righty Michael King who pitched his best in the postseason as well.

Neither of those players can receive a qualifying offer, making them even more attractive to teams, and they headline a group of starters who should sign before a December lockout.

Who are the biggest trade candidates this offseason?

Olney: The trade market really won't gain clarity until after the next CBA is settled, except in a few isolated cases; I've heard Seattle is poking around to assess how its surplus in pitching might be used to add a bat. But generally, teams are going to be very wary of making trades without being able to attach appropriate value to the players proposed in deals -- and no one will be able to do that with confidence until they know what the financial system looks like.

Passan: At the top of the list is Tampa Bay ace Drew Rasmussen, whose $20 million salary would push the Rays' payroll above their 2026 level without making another move. Will their World Series run encourage ownership to push the payroll and keep Rasmussen around for another run, or is the ability to clean up in a trade too strong to turn down?

The Astros, under new GM Randy Flores, have to decide what to do with shortstop Jeremy Pena a year before he reaches free agency. Multiple candidates for the GM job had suggested a rebuild would be the best course of action. The Los Angeles Angels, after trading Jose Soriano at the deadline, still have left-hander Reid Detmers and shortstop Zach Neto -- and the new head of baseball operations there has a mess to clean up. Arizona could move Ketel Marte -- if he's willing to waive his no-trade clause. And while William Contreras isn't going anywhere even though he is nearing free agency, the World Series champion Brewers will at least listen on closer Trevor Megill.

What are you hearing the pending lockout could mean for the pace of offseason moves?

Jorge Castillo: The expectation is it's going to be 2021 all over again. Five years ago, the last few days of November were a frenzy as teams committed $1.9 billion to free agents before the previous collective bargaining agreement expired. Nine players signed nine-figure contracts, led by Corey Seager's 10-year, $325 million deal with the Texas Rangers.

While Tarik Skubal, the top free agent this winter, is expected to sign a deal north of that before the lockout, this free agent class isn't nearly as deep. Players are going to fly off the board anyway.

Gonzalez: Ditto on the amount of action, and, to emphasize: the perception among executives is that this is generally a very weak crop of free agents. Outside of Teruaki Sato, a 27-year-old Japanese third baseman who's expected to be posted in the coming days and could one day be a Triple Crown threat, it's slim pickings on offense.

Aside from Skubal, the best starting pitcher available might be Kaima Taira, a 5-foot-8 right-hander with a vast repertoire. The markets for Sato, Taira and fellow Japanese star Hiromi Itoh will dominate a lot of the conversation over these next few weeks. But there will be a lot of action around them.

Has a Rays-Brewers World Series impacted how teams are approaching the offseason?

Passan: Not really. The Rays and Brewers have been regarded as excellent organizations for the last decade. Getting to the World Series is validation, yes, but their approaches are well-known and have been for years. Teams with more resources aren't suddenly going to give away the advantage that accompanies higher payrolls simply because the Rays, Brewers and Cleveland Guardians found success with lower ones. If the demand for players who put the ball in play or are elite baserunners rise precipitously, sure, we'll entertain the idea that there's some sort of an effect. But we'll take the under.

Rogers: It's too early to tell, but there is some chatter about the way those teams put the ball in play having a ripple effect in the sport. If anything, they serve as a reminder that there is more than one way to win a game and the more diverse options you have at the plate or on the mound, the better. Winning without just slugging home runs has taken some notice around the league.

What are the Dodgers most likely to do in the offseason after being dethroned this postseason?

Gonzalez: Outside of a pursuit of Skubal and a restocking of their bullpen -- Alex Vesia and Evan Phillips are among their free agents, and the Dodgers will probably be interested in a reunion -- there might not be a whole lot. Even without Skubal, the Dodgers possess enviable pitching depth.

Their entire starting lineup is under contract. And though their front office will spend a lot of time debating the merits of a younger position-player group, that might ultimately happen internally -- with the likes of Josue De Paula, Alex Freeland and, when he recovers from elbow surgery, Dalton Rushing mixing in. Could a blockbuster deal for a young, controllable, upper-eschelon position player materialize? Certainly. But those are always difficult.

Olney: The postseason demonstrated that the Dodgers have to start thinking about reshaping their position player group, to get younger and more athletic. But that will be challenging, with so many of their veterans under contract. The most obvious trade candidate in their position player group is Teoscar Hernandez, because as he gets older and his defensive skills naturally decline, there is no out for him at the DH spot, with the presence of Shohei Ohtani.

After both seasons ended short of where they hoped, how are the two New York teams likely to approach the offseason?

Castillo: The Mets will be the more aggressive of the two clubs, and it starts with Tarik Skubal. They are considered the favorite to land the prize of this free agent class for two reasons: (A) there's a clear need for a top-tier starting pitcher, (B) they're one of the very few teams willing to pay top dollar for premier free agents.

The Yankees have a few decisions to make. Closer David Bednar is a free agent. They'll likely look for an upgrade at third base. Jazz Chisholm Jr. and Trent Grisham are as good as gone so they'll need to figure out center field and second base. But there are internal options for all those uncertainties.

The Yankees believe they have a championship contender with a few tweaks. The Mets, after missing the playoffs consecutive seasons, are still laying the foundation.

Passan: Both have work to do. The back end of the Yankees' bullpen is nearly empty, second and third base are unclear and while the Yankees have more offensive talent than most, finding spots for them leaves the team vulnerable defensively. The Yankees will be good again because of their starting pitching and star bats, but getting to a championship level will necessitate more.

The Mets just want to get back to the playoffs, and they've got a handful of pieces capable of getting them there. Signing Skubal would be a great place to start. Beyond that, they need significant bullpen help, another starting arm and two more productive bats to be able to say they're on the level of the Braves and Phillies, let alone the Marlins and Nationals, both of whom took steps forward in 2026.

Which other teams does the industry think could make a splash this winter?

Olney: The Cubs, Mariners and Padres -- flush with new owner cash -- and after the lockout, the Angels. The Cubs have a group of veterans in their lineup who are win-now players, like Alex Bregman, Dansby Swanson, Nico Hoerner and Michael Busch, and they need to match that by enhancing their pitching. The question with so many teams is whether or not their respective owners will green-light moves -- I've heard estimates of anywhere from 12 to 18 teams will be largely inclined to sit out November, but of course, that could change if front offices successfully lobby for adding payroll before the lockout.

Rogers: Almost by definition, the Cubs have to be active -- otherwise they won't be able to field a pitching staff. With several pitchers coming off injuries and a bunch of free agent arms, the Cubs need bodies. They'll entertain almost anyone which also means circling back to some of their own guys. Clay Holmes and David Peterson could be candidates for a return engagement. Some believe the Mariners will also do some reshaping of their roster after such a down year.

With Halloween weekend in the rearview mirror, the next major event on the calendar is American Thanksgiving -- and all the important clues that will give us in the race for the Stanley Cup playoffs.

To get the week started, it's a four-pack of games Monday, with a wide array of storylines.

Vegas Golden Knights at Boston Bruins

7 p.m. ET (NHL Network) | VGK -112, O/U: 6.5

In Monday's marquee matchup, the defending Western Conference champs take on the current Atlantic Division leaders. Stathletes gives this matchup a 0.76% chance of occurring as the 2027 Stanley Cup Final, which ranks 40th.

This will also be a homecoming for Vegas center Jack Eichel (North Chelmsford, Massachusetts, and Boston University) and defenseman Noah Hanifin (Boston and Boston College). Eichel has nine goals and 15 assists in 22 career games against the Bruins (with Buffalo and Vegas), and Hanifin has five goals and 12 assists in 22 games (with Carolina, Calgary and Vegas).

Thanks in large part to Jeremy Swayman -- Eichel's and Hanifin's Olympic teammate -- the Bruins are allowing the fourth-fewest goals per game in the league (2.40), and they are a perfect 9-0-0 in games in which they score three or more goals.

Detroit Red Wings at Florida Panthers

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | FLA -175, O/U: 5.5

The Panthers, who are on a three-game winning streak, welcome the Red Wings to Sunrise. Although they are 8-4-2 overall, they have yet to win against an Atlantic Division opponent, going 0-2-0 thus far. Florida has two players in the top 15 in scoring: Matthew Tkachuk (tied for ninth with 20 points through 14 games) and Seth Jones (tied for 14th with 18 through 14).

One has to scroll down a bit farther to find Detroit's leading scorer, Alex DeBrincat, who is tied for 35th with 15 points in 14 games.

The Wings have a 3-1-0 record in games in which they serve fewer penalty minutes than their opponent. This will be a factor, given that the Panthers have the NHL's ninth-ranked power play, clicking along at a 24.2% rate.

Colorado Avalanche at Chicago Blackhawks

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | COL -230, O/U: 5.5

On paper, this one doesn't appear to be the most competitive pairing. But, the Bruins were minus-225 against the Blackhawks on Saturday and narrowly escaped with an OT win.

This is the first of four matchups between these clubs this season, and they won't meet again until Feb. 28 -- when, presumably, each team will have a different makeup thanks to trade season.

The Avs are paced offensively by Nathan MacKinnon (24 points through 14 games), Martin Necas (18 through 14) and Artturi Lehkonen (17 through 14), while the Blackhawks have a tie atop their stat sheet between Connor Bedard (nine points through eight games) and Patrick Kane (nine through 14).

Calgary Flames at San Jose Sharks

9 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | SJ -135, O/U: 6.5

This was supposed to be the season in which the Sharks return to the playoffs -- and it still might be, but games against seemingly outmatched opponents have slipped away from them.

San Jose will want to stay out of the penalty box as much as possible; Calgary brings the NHL's No. 2 power play (33.3%) to the SAP Center, including three power-play goals apiece already for Matvei Gridin and Morgan Frost.

The Sharks are led in scoring by Macklin Celebrini (16 points through 13 games) and Will Smith (10 through 15), their dynamic duo.

stories.headline: Kimi Antonelli is F1 champion. But why didn't he get his trophy in Mexico City?
stories.summary: Kimi Antonelli is F1 world champion, but he won't get his trophy until December. Why does the sport still deny its champions their crowning moment?
stories.body:
There was one rather significant thing missing from Kimi Antonelli's world championship celebrations in Mexico City: the world championship trophy itself.

Despite becoming the youngest champion in Formula 1 history, the Italian will have to wait until Dec. 12 to get his hands on the prize he has spent his life chasing. That is because, unlike almost every other major sporting competition, F1 does not hand its championship trophy to the winner at the moment of victory. Instead, Antonelli will receive it while wearing a tuxedo, in a sterile hall, at the FIA's annual prize-giving gala dinner in Shanghai in December, six weeks after clinching the title.

It is one of F1's more peculiar traditions, denying the sport the sort of iconic sporting image synonymous with its biggest prizes. Think of the World Cup, the Super Bowl's Vince Lombardi Trophy or NHL's Stanley Cup, just to name three. The moment of triumph and the presentation of the trophy are inseparable. It doesn't have to be a conventional trophy, either. The Masters has turned the previous winner presenting the new winner a green blazer one of the most iconic images in all of sports.

F1's championship trophy, by contrast, seems almost an afterthought. Many fans would struggle to recognise it, which seems crazy for the series which is the pinnacle of motor racing.

It is a shame, too, because it is an impressive piece of silverware. Introduced in 1995, the trophy is made of sterling silver with gold detailing and features the signatures of Formula 1's world champions, stretching back to Giuseppe Farina in 1950.

So why wasn't it visible in Mexico City?

The answer lies in the divide between Formula 1 and its governing body, the FIA.

While F1, owned by Liberty Media, controls the commercial side of the championship, the FIA oversees its sporting and regulatory affairs. The world championship trophy falls under the FIA's jurisdiction -- Antonelli on Sunday officially became the FIA Formula 1 world champion - and its regulations stipulate that it must be presented at the governing body's annual gala.

Liberty Media has been keen to make more of the championship trophy. Sources have told ESPN discussions over a change this year did take place -- as they have for successive years now -- that the trophy be presented to Antonelli the moment he won it this year. However, as has also happened in previous seasons, it was agreed the FIA would stick with the convention of previous seasons and opt against doing anything radically different this time around.

- Antonelli makes F1 history as youngest world champion with maiden title

- Verstappen wins Mexico City GP for Red Bull; Antonelli seals historic title

- Antonelli's historic F1 title: Every record broken and milestone reached

The FIA has long argued that presenting the trophy at its gala is important to the occasion's prestige. The event celebrates champions from across motorsport, including rallying, endurance racing and karting, with the presence of Formula 1's world champion regarded as an important attraction for the younger winners.

There is also a sporting justification, as race results can be challenged or altered after the chequered flag, potentially changing the outcome of a championship. The FIA prefers to wait until those matters are settled before handing over its biggest prize.

That argument has some merit, although less so when Antonelli has wrapped up the championship with four races still to run. It rather falls apart altogether when considering what happens at every grand prix as it is the exact opposite of the practice the FIA puts forward in that instance. Individual race trophies are handed out immediately after the finish, despite those results also being subject to protests, penalties and subsequent disqualifications. If a result changes, the trophies simply change hands.

Look no further than Sunday's race in Mexico City for an example. Antonelli was clutching his third-place Mexico City Grand Prix trophy in his hands at different points during his celebratory moments on the podium and the ceremony which followed. That despite the fact a post-race penalty or protest could have moved him down the order after the fact -- it wouldn't have stopped him being champion, but it would have meant he should not have been on the podium. And yet, he did not have the world championship trophy in his hand for that exact same reason.

There is little reason why the championship should be treated differently to an individual race, especially when the current practice stops the trophy becoming a prize that champions can share with fans in the celebratory moments.

It seems a missed opportunity for a sport which has spent the past decade transforming the way it presents itself to the world. F1 has embraced new audiences, new technology and new ways of celebrating its biggest moments, yet its most prestigious prize remains tied to an awards dinner.

Antonelli will undoubtedly enjoy getting his hands on the trophy in Shanghai. But the moment he became world champion, surrounded by his Mercedes team and thousands of celebrating fans in Mexico City, has already passed and it is a moment Formula 1 cannot recreate.

stories.headline: Messi brings Miami back to stun Revs, clinch Champions Cup spot
stories.summary: Inter Miami CF beat the New England Revolution 2-1 on Sunday in Foxborough, Massachusetts, with Lionel Messi once again providing the magic touch, this time to ensure his team's spot in the 2027 Concacaf Champions Cup.
stories.body:
Inter Miami CF beat the New England Revolution 2-1 on Sunday in Foxborough, Massachusetts, with Lionel Messi once again providing the magic touch, this time to ensure his team's spot in the 2027 Concacaf Champions Cup.

The win also helped Miami leapfrog the Revs into second place in the Eastern Conference with one game remaining in the MLS regular season.

"It makes me very happy for the players and for the club, we are on the side of contributing things," Miami manager Cristian González said after the game. "We are at a club that is in continuous growth, I have players committed to us. We needed to win and we challenged ourselves on what kind of team we wanted to be."

The Revolution edged out Inter Miami in the first half, registering six total shots, five corner kicks and generating an expected goals of .75, but the match went to the break tied 0-0.

Dániel Gazdag then opened up the scoring in the initial minutes of the second half, connecting with Ilay Feingold inside the box before finding the back of the net.

Miami found a way to respond to Gazdag's strike with a goal from Germán Berterame -- set up by a deft backward header from Messi -- in the 69th minute. González then bolstered Inter Miami's attack after drawing level, substituting in Luis Suárez, who had started Miami's last 25 games.

"We knew we were going up against a rival that tries to seek out duels where they defend high, so the possibility of changes was to have depth, look for the spaces, and the one-on-one matchups. We struggled with ball possession, which at times was very passive," said González. "My message to the players is I need everyone. In this case, we believed we needed to make some changes.

"This doesn't mean this is the team that's going to start the playoffs. Everyone shows me they're eager to want to play."

Messi doubled the score for Inter Miami, dribbling past defenders outside the box and smashing a trademark low, left-footed shot past Revs keeper Matt Turner.

The Revolution almost found their way back for a draw, but Ian Fray's own goal was quickly ruled offside to let Miami off the hook after it looked like Messi's heroics had been undone.

Ultimately, it was Messi's goal that clinched Inter Miami a spot in the 2027 Champions Cup. Had Miami lost or tied the game against the Revs they would have had work left to do on Decision Day on Nov. 7 to get into North America's top club competition.

"I have no doubt that he's the best of all," González said of Messi. None of them can compare to him when it comes to respect for his colleagues. Leo at his age and what he does, from my point of view, deserves the MVP and also the Ballon d'Or. I hope he can achieve it."

Inter Miami now joins Nashville SC, the Revs and the Vancouver Whitecaps in the 2027 Concacaf Champions Cup. The winner of the 2026 MLS Cup will also have a place in the Champions Cup.

The Herons now have 59 points from 33 games, and will finish the regular season with a home game against Charlotte FC that will have seeding implications ahead of the MLS playoffs.

stories.headline: How the Golden State Valkyries won the 2026 WNBA title in just two years
stories.summary: When Golden State joined the WNBA, the owner said the team would win a title within five years. The Valkyries did it in two.
stories.body:
SAN FRANCISCO -- Almost exactly two years ago, Natalie Nakase sat across from Golden State owner Joe Lacob for her job interview to become the head coach of the WNBA's newest team, the Valkyries. It was October 2024, and Nakase had walked into the interview with notes on why she would be the best fit, her vision for how to build a team and what set her apart from her colleagues.

But the first 10 minutes of the conversation were led by Lacob: He told Nakase he likes to set incredibly high goals and shared how he plans to achieve them. Nakase sat up straighter and leaned in a few inches closer, enticed by Lacob's work ethic.

Near the end of the conversation, Lacob told Nakase the ultimate goal, the same one he had shared in the news conference announcing the creation of the team a year earlier: "We're going to win a championship in five years."

She slammed her fists on the table in front of them.

"Hell yeah, we're gonna win a championship," she said.

On Saturday, the Golden State Valkyries did just that, beating the Atlanta Dream 68-63 in Game 7 of the WNBA Finals to win their first title.

Lacob and Nakase were wrong about one thing, though. The Valkyries didn't win their first championship in five years. They did it in two.

"I walked out of that conversation with Joe like, 'I want to work for him,'" Nakase said. "More than that, I want to win that first championship for him."

After the interview, Nakase immediately called her mentors, asking them how she could deliver on Lacob's aspirations. Their biggest piece of advice was to build a clear culture, and do it with competitors who would sacrifice anything for the group.

Along with general manager Ohemaa Nyanin, Nakase set the identity she wanted for her team: scrappy, defensive-minded, no egos. The Valkyries built the team their way, facing external scrutiny nearly every step of the way. People gawked -- or even laughed -- at Lacob's proclamation. But Nakase stood strong in her belief, and in his.

Sitting next to the championship trophy with a beer in her hand Saturday, Nakase was asked if winning the title felt as she imagined it would.

"F--- yeah."

TOGETHER, NYANIN AND Nakase handpicked the players who make up Golden State's roster. During the 2024 expansion draft, the Valkyries acquired Veronica Burton, the gritty two-way guard, and Kayla Thornton, a reigning WNBA champion -- two cornerstones of the franchise -- as well as Cecilia Zandalasini, an Italian national. Tiffany Hayes, a former Sixth Player of the Year, signed in free agency, and Janelle Salaun, a French forward, signed on a training camp roster. The Valkyries used their No. 5 pick in 2025 on Juste Jocyte -- a 19-year-old from Lithuania who stayed overseas that year.

Again, their decisions were questioned. Without a star, and without a history of any success, external expectations for the Valkyries were low.

But in the 2025 postseason, this group made history, propelling the Valkyries to become the first expansion franchise in WNBA history to make the playoffs in its first season. The Valkyries were swept by the Minnesota Lynx in the first round, but it laid the foundation for what the team could build on, and made Golden State an attractive landing place for free agents.

For more than a year, the Valkyries knew whom they wanted to prioritize. Gabby Williams was part of Nyanin's original vision of the team, and Nakase met with Williams in 2025 in Turkey to pitch her on coming to Golden State. But the Seattle Storm cored Williams that offseason, guaranteeing Seattle exclusive negotiating rights with the French national. Williams remembers when she heard Lacob make his proclamation in 2023. "I was impressed, and I was enticed. It was like, this is a team I could want to play for one day," Williams said. "I thought I would finish my career in Seattle, but hearing that made me think a little bit. This guy is not playing around; he wants to win. That was eye-opening to me."

When Williams became a free agent, the Valkyries contacted her again, and Lacob joined Nakase and Nyanin in the recruitment.

"He said, 'This is why we are going to win. This is why it would be silly for you to go anywhere else. This is why we're going to have longevity. I want to build dynasties here,'" Williams said.

"Who doesn't want to come to something like that? We play this game to win championships. I've never won one, and at this point in my career, that is the top priority. ... I was so convinced that I would not win anywhere else."

One day after signing Williams, the Valkyries made another trajectory-shifting acquisition, landing Kiah Stokes after she spent four seasons and won three titles with Las Vegas, where she played alongside A'ja Wilson every day and under Nakase for one year. After Iliana Rupert announced that she would miss the 2026 season due to pregnancy, Stokes started every game, defending Angel Reese in the Finals.

Nyanin knew that these players could unlock a new level of her team. What has surprised the GM, though, is how quickly it has come together.

"You just never know if that's going to work out," Nyanin said.

It has. Williams, who was named Finals MVP thanks to a 30-point performance in Game 7, is having the best season of her career. She averaged a career-best 14.4 points and shot 34.2% from 3 -- and also finished second in Defensive Player of the Year voting and received WNBA All-Defensive first-team honors. She became the engine for Golden State's top-ranked defense, while also stepping up to be the shotmaker the Valkyries needed.

"The best part has been coming to work every day and enjoying it. Like, actually, that's a huge part of contending," Williams said. "When the playoffs started, our motivation was just -- we didn't want to stop playing together. We wanted to go as deep as we could because we knew this is the last time we could have a group like this. It's been really healing for me. It's made this season really special."

Down late in a win-or-go-home Game 3 in the first round against the Dallas Wings, Thornton pulled Burton, Williams and Kaila Charles into a huddle beneath their basket. They put their arms around each other and took a collective breath.

"It's just one of those things where [it was] an awareness of what we need," Burton said. "And in that moment, we needed to take an exhale and be together and just be present. ... That's pouring into each other and building each other up."

As Nyanin watched from the tunnel -- and as that sigh fueled their comeback and offered a glimpse of the composure Golden State, a team with no All-WNBA player selections, has possessed since its inception, Nyanin knew that all of the pieces she put together fit perfectly.

"That was the epitome of things we have said to them here and there," Nyanin said. "In that moment, all of the little things we have put together, I took a breath as well just to say yes, they will fight with each other and for each other. That's exactly why I am doing the job I am doing."

NAKASE WOULDN'T LET her players pick up a ball for the first three days of training camp this season.

There was no shooting, no running plays, no offense. The first three days of camp were dedicated to defense.

"That's when I knew this was going to be different," Burton said.

Those early sessions set the tone for what Nakase would demand: consistent defensive intensity, attention to detail and execution on the game plan. It also gave her players a taste of the kind of coach she is -- one who plays battle sounds during practice and calls her players "killers," doesn't allow for celebrations, and believes that cursing just means you're telling the truth.

Even when Nakase's behavior seems jarring -- or as she puts it, extreme -- she has built an environment that encourages her players to speak up and feel respected. It's why they so willingly buy into Nakase's vision and style.

"She's so authentic," Williams said. "We know her intentions are to put us in the best position to win. ... She's passionate. And sometimes we laugh at her, but we also check on her ... it's the love we have for each other."

When Williams arrived in Golden State, she told Nakase that sometimes her delivery was confusing. Others have told Nakase that they needed more time to celebrate the smaller wins. Her coaching staff urged her to take more care of herself so she can be a better leader.

All of this experience has led the Valkyries here, to their first title. Nakase's focus on defense made Golden State's unit the top ranked in the league through the regular season -- holding opponents to a league-low 75.1 points per game -- and second best in the playoffs. Stokes had 31 blocked shots this postseason, tied with Lisa Leslie for the most in WNBA history.

And her players' feedback has pushed Nakase to be a better version of herself -- and helped turn around the Finals when Golden State trailed 2-1. After the first three games of the series, she gave herself an F-minus score on her coaching because her communication was poor. So she turned to her players to see how she -- and in turn they -- could be better.

"You can give the best scheme in the world, but if your players don't want to follow it, it's not going to be successful," Stokes said. "Her willingness to listen to us and our ideas about what we think we're best at and what we can do, that's one thing that has jumped out to me; her willingness to adapt to her players."

Heading into Game 4, Nakase inserted Hayes and Kaila Charles into the starting lineup in place of Thornton and Zandalasini, respectively. Charles finished the game with a plus-14, and Hayes added 13 points -- and the change led to a massive momentum shift in the series, with the Valkyries taking the next two games.

"The best thing about our team is no one cares who starts, no one cares," Nakase said. "We can do that because we have a really selfless team, ego-less team."

"She's a great coach for a reason," Charles. "We trust our coach, so whatever she sees, we'll execute."

As Nakase walked out of her first interview with Lacob, she pledged to herself not to let his WNBA team fail. When she began to work alongside Nyanin, she promised her that they wouldn't let each other fail. As she opened up each season with her players, Nakase made sure they had every piece of support they needed.

All of this has led to history, and the Valkyries winning a title far sooner than anyone -- even Lacob -- could have ever predicted.

"Of course this is unbelievable," Lacob said Saturday night as the Valkyries celebrated. "Two years? It's insane."

stories.headline: Chris Fagan to join the Blues as director of coaching in 2027
stories.summary: Triple premeirship coach Chris Fagan has made the call on his AFL future, joining Carlton as their director of coaching for 2027.
stories.body:
Triple premeirship coach Chris Fagan has made the call on his AFL future, joining Carlton as their director of coaching for 2027.

The 65-year-old stepped down as Brisbane's senior coach after the club's 2026 premiership win -- it's third in a row -- with an aim to return closer to family.

Announced by the Blues on Saturday morning, Fagan will oversee a matchday role and begin mentoring the coaching panel to "establish development pathways for the coaches and help drive an elite, sustainable football program".

Fagan said he was looking forward to making a "real impact" at the Blues.

"While I loved my 10 years as a Senior Coach, this is a role I am passionate about and where I know I can have a real impact in this next phase of my football career," Fagan said in a statement.

"Supporting people to get the absolute best out of themselves is what I love most about football, so the chance to now be able to do that on a full-time basis is incredibly exciting. I can't wait to connect with each person in the football department, and in particular work closely with Josh to help every coach and player be the best Carlton person they can possibly be.

"In all my conversations with [the club] before accepting the role, what resonated strongly was how aligned they were on how to make Carlton a great football club. They shared a clear vision of evolving Carlton into a club that can contend but most importantly, they understand there is still significant work to do to get there.

"To have the senior leadership of a football club share such clarity in their direction, combined with a role that gives me genuine purpose, makes joining Carlton an opportunity too good to pass up."

Meanwhile Carlton's GM of Football Chris Davies said the appointment was an important one to support first-time senior coach Josh Fraser.

"We want to build our football club around good people and they do not come any better than Chris Fagan," Davies said.

"Few in the game have his wealth of experience and ability to connect with and get the best out of those around him. Most importantly, he is a proven winner who knows what it takes to build a consistently high-performing environment.

"Chris and Josh have built a connection in recent weeks over a shared philosophy of putting people first and building a program the right way. With Chris on board, Josh will be well supported, our coaches will be well developed and our program will continue to build the clarity and discipline required to be truly elite.

"We can't wait to welcome Chris and his wife Ursula, their daughters Jessica and Ellen and the entire Fagan family to Carlton."

...more to come.

stories.headline: 'Do everything': Walsh credits Walters chat for return
stories.summary: Reece Walsh says it's "a blessing" to be a sponge around his Australia fullback competitor James Tedesco as he reveals how he got fit for the World Cup.
stories.body:
When Reece Walsh spoke to Australia coach Kevin Walters in August after ankle surgery concerning his World Cup hopes, there were no guarantees.

It is why the Kangaroos fullback's ice pack on his left ankle after the 66-6 win over Cook Islands on Saturday night, in his second man of the match display in the tournament, was a symbol of his commitment and drive beyond the flamboyance he shows on the field.

Walsh, 24, took a knock to the same ankle against the Aitu in Townsville that he suffered a high grade syndesmosis injury to while playing for Brisbane on August 15.

He played through the discomfort to set up five tries, vindicating all the hard yards in rehab that got him selected for his first World Cup.

"I spoke to Kevvie early and I said if you are thinking about picking me, I am going to do everything I can to get back," Walsh said

"He said, 'Walshy, nothing is guaranteed. If you get fit and get your ankle right I will have a look at it'. I didn't go on holidays. To be honest I worked really hard to put myself in a position to get back in this team."

Walsh spent three or four days at the Broncos with rehab and physio gurus such as Lindsay Self and Luke Anning, whom he praised for assisting him in their own holiday breaks.

They told him not to be overly concerned if he suffered a bump on the ankle.

"They generally say that when you have the tightrope (fixation surgery) and rod through it that it is stronger than it normally is," Walsh said.

"I was bound to get a bang on it. I didn't get one in the first game and I got one out there (against Cook Islands) so I feel like it was a good test of strength of it."

Walsh is in a fullback battle with Sydney Roosters captain James Tedesco, who was excellent in the 36-22 win over Fiji last week in the match Walsh did not play.

Walsh would widely be considered to have his nose slightly in front to play in the semi-final against Samoa at Allianz Stadium on Sunday night, but the coach has given him no indication.

"He actually hasn't. One thing we spoke about being in this environment and this team is nothing is guaranteed," Walsh said.

"We are all here to learn off each other and help each other get to the ultimate goal of winning the World Cup.

"Whatever Kevvie wants to do we are all going to support him. No one has dropped their lip or had a sour taste."

Walsh, also a Queensland representative, is a sponge taking in Tedesco's wisdom as he lives out his boyhood Kangaroos dream.

"When you look at this jersey I feel like it is the pinnacle of our game," he said.

"Origin level is so amazing but I also feel like as a kid you play in Queensland or NSW to make Australia.

"I wear that jersey with pride. I go out there to represent not just myself but our nation and my family and the people that set me up to be here.

"I feel like being in camp with Teddy has been such a blessing for me.

"To see someone like himself, the way he prepares, the way he carries himself and the character he is ... I am learning so much."

stories.headline: Regis Le Bris retains Sunderland confidence despite bad run - report
stories.summary: Sunderland boss Regis Le Bris retains the full support of the club's board and remains central to their plans, the Press Association understands.
stories.body:
Sunderland boss Regis Le Bris retains the full support of the club's board and remains central to their plans, the Press Association understands.

The 50-year-old Frenchman has come under increasing pressure following the Black Cats' poor start to the Premier League season as the club sit bottom of the table with one win from nine matches.

Saturday's 3-1 defeat at Coventry extended Sunderland's winless league run to seven games, while they have collected just one point from five on the road.

The club's hierarchy recognise fans' frustrations and share their disappointment with some below-par performances, but believe Le Bris can turn their fortunes around.

The former Lorient head coach's stock could not have been much higher in the summer.

After leading the club to promotion via the play-offs, he guided them to an impressive seventh-placed finish in their first season back in the top flight after an eight-year absence, delivering European football for the first time in 53 years.

The Black Cats have made an unbeaten start to their Europa League campaign, with wins against AZ Alkmaar and Torreense and more recently a draw in Poland against Lech Poznan.

The added fixtures appear to have taken a toll on the players' top-flight performances, but Sunderland's hierarchy feel their ambitions are best served by maintaining stability and adopting a collective responsibility.

The Black Cats are next in action on Thursday against Europa League opponents Dinamo Zagreb at home before they face Chelsea at the Stadium of Light in the Premier League on Sunday.
